profile.name: Mina S.
profile.tagline: First-year Electrical Engineering student at the University of Toronto, exploring power systems, embedded computing, cybersecurity, and responsible AI.
profile.definition: To me, digital citizenship means combining technical skill with responsibility. It includes checking information before sharing it, protecting privacy, using technology ethically, and contributing to online spaces in ways that make them safer and more respectful.
profile.mission: My mission is to grow as an engineer and digital citizen at the same time. I want the way I learn, build, and communicate online to reflect curiosity, care, and cybersecurity awareness.
profile.aboutTitle: First-year Electrical Engineering student at the University of Toronto
aboutText: I am Mina Soliman, a first-year Electrical Engineering student at the University of Toronto. I am interested in power systems, embedded computing, cybersecurity, and the design of technology people can understand and trust.

Cybersecurity is one of the areas that excites me most because it connects technical design with trust, privacy, and accountability. That interest naturally connects to digital citizenship, which gives me a framework for how I want to participate online.
This website brings those interests together. It tracks how I learn, reflect, and contribute so my growth in digital citizenship stays visible, measurable, and grounded in real habits.

personalGoals: Keep source verification consistent enough that I can explain why I trust what I share.
Treat privacy settings as a repeated maintenance task instead of a one-time setup step.
Use AI as a support tool only when I can still account for accuracy, authorship, and impact.
Contribute at least one useful resource, walkthrough, or peer-support action every week.
codeOfConduct: Verify before sharing, especially when content is emotionally charged or urgent.
Protect private information and ask for consent before reposting or forwarding someone else's content.
Credit ideas, code, and creative work clearly.
Use disagreement to clarify, not to embarrass or escalate.
Pause when a tool saves time but weakens responsibility.
principles: I will verify information before sharing it.
I will use technology in ways that help rather than harm.
I will protect my privacy and respect other people's privacy.
I will contribute positively to online communities.
I will be transparent about the role of AI and automation in my work.
I will practice consent in digital spaces, not just compliance.
I will reflect on how my digital habits affect myself and others.

reflections.title: Designing privacy into a prototype before adding features
content: While sketching a small browser-based prototype, I caught myself treating privacy as a settings screen I could add near the end. I restarted the plan by listing what data the idea truly needed, what could stay on the device, and what should never be collected.
The change made the project simpler. Privacy by design is not only about preventing harm; it can also force clearer decisions about what a product is actually for.
reflections.takeaway: The change made the project simpler.

reflections.title: Threat modeling is a technical form of empathy
content: My first threat-modeling exercise felt like a list of things that could go wrong. It became more useful when I stopped thinking only about attackers and started asking who could be confused, excluded, pressured, or exposed by an ordinary design decision.
Security thinking gets stronger when it includes the experience of the person using the system. Anticipating misuse and anticipating friction are both ways of taking people seriously.
reflections.takeaway: Security thinking gets stronger when it includes the experience of the person using the system.

reflections.title: Cleaning a repository is part of communicating responsibly
content: A repository can technically work while still making the next person search through unclear names, generated files, and missing context. I treated a cleanup session as communication work: organize the structure, explain the purpose, and make the useful path obvious.
Good documentation respects other people's time. A clear project also makes it easier for me to notice what I actually understand and what I have only been carrying forward.
reflections.takeaway: Good documentation respects other people's time.

reflections.title: Accessibility belongs inside digital citizenship
content: I reviewed a form using only a keyboard and quickly found places where the visual design looked finished but the interaction did not. Labels, focus order, contrast, and motion preferences determine who can actually participate.
Accessibility is not an optional polish layer. If digital citizenship is about contributing to spaces responsibly, access has to be part of the definition from the beginning.
reflections.takeaway: Accessibility is not an optional polish layer.

reflections.title: Checking the links behind a persuasive video
content: A polished video used charts and confident narration to make its conclusion feel settled. I followed the sources in the description and found that one link did not support the number shown, while another was several years older than the narration implied.
Production quality can make a claim feel verified before any verification happens. I now treat confidence, editing, and visual polish as presentation signals—not evidence signals.
reflections.takeaway: Production quality can make a claim feel verified before any verification happens.

reflections.title: Reviewing my digital footprint before the next school year
content: As I look ahead to starting electrical engineering in Canada, I wanted to review what I am publicly attaching to my name online. That meant checking bios, old posts, shared profiles, and the tone of the spaces where I participate most.

The goal was not to erase personality, but to make sure my digital footprint reflects the kind of learner and community member I want to be: curious, responsible, and increasingly aware of cybersecurity and digital citizenship.
reflections.takeaway: The goal was not to erase personality, but to make sure my digital footprint reflects the kind of learner and community member I want to be: curious, responsible, and increasingly aware of cybersecurity and digital citizenship.

reflections.title: Cross-checking AI summaries before I trust them
content: AI summaries are useful for orientation, but they often compress uncertainty out of a topic. This week I started checking every summary against at least one primary source before I reuse any claim.
That extra step slowed me down slightly, but it improved my confidence and made my notes more accurate. Convenience is only ethical when it still leaves room for responsibility.
reflections.takeaway: That extra step slowed me down slightly, but it improved my confidence and made my notes more accurate.

reflections.title: Reducing passive screen time after 9 PM
content: I noticed that tired scrolling made me less thoughtful about what I liked, shared, and clicked. I replaced late-night scrolling with a short shutdown checklist and one intentional article or video.
The change helped me separate rest from distraction and made my online time feel more chosen than automatic.
reflections.takeaway: The change helped me separate rest from distraction and made my online time feel more chosen than automatic.

reflections.title: Revisiting privacy defaults on every new app
content: I used to treat privacy setup as a one-time task, but every new app quietly adds fresh decisions. I now check visibility, permissions, contact sync, and notification settings before I start using a service regularly.
That routine turns privacy from a vague value into a repeatable behavior.
reflections.takeaway: That routine turns privacy from a vague value into a repeatable behavior.

reflections.title: Writing clearer and kinder replies in group chats
content: Short messages travel fast, and tone gets flattened easily. I started pausing before sending corrections or reminders, especially in group chats where public friction can grow quickly.
Being concise does not require being sharp. Clear and respectful replies reduce noise and help people stay engaged.
reflections.takeaway: Being concise does not require being sharp.

reflections.title: When productivity tools become distractions
content: I spent too much time tuning tools that were supposed to save time. The problem was not the apps themselves, but the way I kept optimizing instead of doing the work.
I now ask whether a tool improves clarity, safety, or output quality. If it mainly adds novelty, I treat it as optional.
reflections.takeaway: I now ask whether a tool improves clarity, safety, or output quality.

reflections.title: Helping classmates cite sources in a shared document
content: A shared study document was growing quickly, but sources were inconsistent. I added a simple citation pattern and a note explaining why link quality matters when notes get reused.
The fix was small, but it made the document more trustworthy and easier for everyone to build on.
reflections.takeaway: The fix was small, but it made the document more trustworthy and easier for everyone to build on.

reflections.title: Slowing down before repeating fast-moving stories
content: A story moved quickly through class chats this week, and my first instinct was to repeat it before I had checked the source. I stopped, looked for the original report, and realized the summary being shared had left out important context.
That moment reminded me that media literacy is often about slowing down when everyone else is speeding up. Accuracy is part of respect.
reflections.takeaway: That moment reminded me that media literacy is often about slowing down when everyone else is speeding up.

reflections.title: Treating password hygiene like regular maintenance
content: I used to think about passwords mostly when a site forced me to update one. This month I started treating password checks as maintenance: review reused passwords, confirm multi-factor authentication, and update recovery methods.
Cybersecurity feels more manageable when I break it into repeated habits instead of waiting for a problem to force a reaction.
reflections.takeaway: Cybersecurity feels more manageable when I break it into repeated habits instead of waiting for a problem to force a reaction.

reflections.title: Resetting notification habits after winter break
content: After winter break I noticed I was reaching for my phone more often than I wanted, mostly because notifications kept interrupting study time. I reviewed which apps actually deserve immediate attention and turned most of the rest into scheduled check-ins.
The change felt small, but it gave me more control over attention and made my online time feel intentional again.
reflections.takeaway: The change felt small, but it gave me more control over attention and made my online time feel intentional again.

reflections.title: Making a shared troubleshooting guide instead of repeating the same fixes
content: A few of us kept running into the same digital tool issues, and I realized I was typing the same answers over and over. I turned those answers into a short shared guide with steps, screenshots, and a note on safe account setup.
Helping once is useful, but documenting a solution can help more people with less friction.
reflections.takeaway: Helping once is useful, but documenting a solution can help more people with less friction.

reflections.title: Using AI for study support without outsourcing my thinking
content: I experimented with using AI to organize study questions and explain unfamiliar terms, but I kept noticing how easy it was to let the tool become the voice of the work. That is useful for speed, but risky for learning.
I set a simple rule for myself: AI can help me start, compare, or check, but it should not replace the part where I explain the idea in my own words.
reflections.takeaway: I set a simple rule for myself: AI can help me start, compare, or check, but it should not replace the part where I explain the idea in my own words.

reflections.title: Reviewing location permissions before convenience becomes the default
content: I realized several apps had access to my location even though they did not need it all the time. It happened gradually because tapping allow was easier than thinking through the tradeoff in the moment.
This reflection pushed me to switch more apps to while-using or never. Privacy is often decided in the tiny moments when convenience asks for less thought.
reflections.takeaway: This reflection pushed me to switch more apps to while-using or never.

reflections.title: Checking captions and claims before reposting
content: I noticed how easy it is to repost something because it sounds right or matches the mood of the moment. This week I made myself read beyond the caption before sharing anything that sounded factual or urgent.
That small pause changed how I think about participation online. Sharing is not neutral when other people may trust the signal I send.
reflections.takeaway: That small pause changed how I think about participation online.

reflections.title: Why I started tracking digital citizenship deliberately
content: I wanted a way to think more seriously about the kind of person I am online, not just the things I post. Digital citizenship felt like the right starting point because it connects behavior, safety, community, and reflection.
Beginning this log made the topic feel practical. Instead of treating good online behavior as a vague ideal, I could start recording choices, patterns, and improvements over time.
reflections.takeaway: Beginning this log made the topic feel practical.

projects.title: Trailhead Customer Support API
projects.description: A grounded FastAPI service that combines Claude-powered conversation with policy retrieval, deterministic business tools, and structured escalation.
projects.impact: It demonstrates how model-driven conversation can stay bounded by tested authorization, business rules, citations, and clear production-safety limits.
projects.role: System architecture, backend implementation, policy grounding, and validation

caseStudy.label: Challenge
caseStudy.title: Let an AI help without letting it invent authority.
caseStudy.copy: A support assistant needs to sound natural while still obeying authorization, refund, citation, and escalation rules. The design challenge was separating conversational flexibility from decisions that must remain deterministic.
points: Escalate when the system reaches its limits

caseStudy.label: Architecture
caseStudy.title: Conversation on top; tested tools underneath.
caseStudy.copy: Claude handles the dialogue, while FastAPI routes sensitive operations through explicit tools. Policy retrieval grounds answers in known material, and structured boundaries keep the model away from direct authority.

caseStudy.label: Evidence
caseStudy.title: The safety story is visible in the repository.
caseStudy.copy: The project documents production limits instead of hiding them. Automated tests exercise expected behavior, escalation is treated as a valid outcome, and the repository makes the implementation available for inspection.

projects.problem: How can a support assistant help without inventing policy or business authority?
projects.built: A FastAPI service combining Claude conversation, policy retrieval, deterministic tools, and structured escalation.
projects.evidence: Tests mock Claude; CI runs the test suite and Ruff. Responses expose citations, tool use, and escalation decisions.
projects.limitations: Read-only fictional business demo. Customer email is a demo authentication stand-in; no refund or cancellation is actually performed.
projects.nextStep: Production use would require signed identity, permission checks, idempotency, audit logs, and explicit action-success responses.
projects.approach: Keep conversation and tool selection in the model while Python owns authorization, calculations, policy retrieval, and escalation rules.
projects.result: Structured support responses distinguish a requested action from a completed action and expose supporting sources.

projects.title: Power Quality Lab
projects.description: A standard-library AC waveform lab that calculates RMS voltage and current, active and apparent power, power factor, and frequency before classifying voltage sag, swell, and low-power-factor conditions.
projects.impact: It turns sampled voltage and current into reproducible engineering evidence while documenting the gap between simulation and a safe, calibrated physical instrument.
projects.problem: How can sampled AC waveforms reveal power-quality problems?
projects.built: A Python waveform lab for RMS, power factor, frequency, sag, swell, and no-load classification.
projects.evidence: Deterministic synthetic waveforms, explicit classification thresholds, and a public unittest suite.
projects.limitations: Simulation only. ADC quantization, isolation, harmonics, calibration drift, and electrical safety are not modeled.
projects.nextStep: A hardware extension would need isolated sensing and calibration in a safe low-voltage test setup.
projects.approach: Preserve simultaneous voltage and current samples; interpolate positive-going zero crossings for frequency; classify against explicit thresholds.
projects.result: A reproducible report of electrical measurements and the classified condition for each synthetic scenario.

projects.title: Microgrid Controller Simulation
projects.description: A deterministic controller that dispatches solar, battery, grid, and load power while enforcing state-of-charge, battery-power, outage, and grid-import constraints.
projects.impact: It makes each dispatch decision inspectable and reports unserved load instead of hiding an impossible energy balance.
projects.problem: How should a microgrid serve demand when solar, battery, and grid power have limits?
projects.built: A deterministic dispatch controller with state-of-charge, battery-power, outage, and grid-import constraints.
projects.evidence: A unittest suite and inspectable dispatch decisions with explicit energy-balance error and unserved load.
projects.limitations: Supervisory simulation only. Voltage dynamics, reactive power, protection, thermal behavior, and communications delay are omitted.
projects.nextStep: A future model could examine the voltage, frequency, and protection dynamics omitted by the supervisory simulation.
projects.approach: Serve load from solar, charge from surplus, discharge within battery limits, and cap imports before reporting unmet demand.
projects.result: Dispatch reports expose each decision and account for unserved load instead of masking an impossible power balance.

projects.title: CAN Bus Anomaly Lab
projects.description: A defensive CAN traffic simulator and explainable rule engine for detecting unknown identifiers, rate spikes, invalid payload ranges, rolling-counter jumps, and timestamp regression.
projects.impact: It demonstrates transparent embedded-network monitoring without transmitting frames or connecting to a safety-critical system.
projects.problem: How can unusual CAN traffic be explained through inspectable rules?
projects.built: A defensive traffic simulator and rule engine for identifiers, timing, payload ranges, and rolling counters.
projects.evidence: Synthetic benign and anomalous traffic, explainable rule findings, and a public unittest suite.
projects.limitations: No physical CAN connection. Static rules can miss slow or context-dependent attacks and need system-specific calibration.
projects.nextStep: A hardware extension would use an isolated development bus and recorded benign traffic within strict safety boundaries.
projects.approach: Validate frames before applying allowlist, rate, payload, and counter rules; report the violated rule and observed value.
projects.result: The documented demo distinguishes a benign baseline from synthetic anomalies without transmitting or modifying frames.

projects.title: Pico 2 W EE Lab Tool
projects.description: A Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W instrument for calibrated power and energy measurement, RC transients, diode characterization, and guided source tests, with an OLED and Wi-Fi dashboard.
projects.impact: A hands-on electrical engineering tool that connects circuit theory, sensor calibration, firmware, and measurement integrity.
projects.problem: How can a compact bench tool measure real circuits and make the limits of each reading visible?
projects.built: Five operating modes on a Pico 2 W, with an INA219, OLED display, Wi-Fi dashboard, and experiment logging.
projects.evidence: The integrated prototype was verified on hardware. Documented RC time constants are 1.076–1.079 s, with calibrated voltage and independently checked shunt current.
projects.limitations: The latest Source Test guard and replacement OLED driver still need device rechecks. Fault monitoring reports conditions; it does not disconnect power.
projects.nextStep: Recheck the Source Test guard and replacement display driver on the hardware, then investigate automated electronic-load stepping.
projects.approach: Use MicroPython to coordinate shared I2C sensing, ADC capture, transistor-controlled RC experiments, settled diode measurements, and shared instrument state for the OLED and Wi-Fi interface.
projects.result: The documented prototype combines Power/Energy, RC Analyzer, Diode Analyzer, internal MCU Temperature, and Guided Source Test modes. Recorded examples include a 1.404 W load and RC capacitance estimates of 1076–1079 µF. These are documented example measurements, not new tests performed for this website.
projects.imageAlt: Original Pico 2 W prototype photo with precise callouts for the controller, INA219 sensor board, OLED display, RC and diode test area, and manual ON/OFF switch.

updates.title: Expanded the peer support mini library with safety and citation resources
updates.why: Classmates needed practical links they could use quickly without sorting through long articles.

updates.title: Drafted a personal guide for responsible AI use
updates.why: I wanted clearer boundaries for when AI helps and when it risks weakening accountability.

updates.title: Created a starter checklist for privacy settings on new apps
updates.why: Default settings often make decisions for me unless I slow down and review them.

updates.title: Revised the site's digital citizenship commitments
updates.why: The values needed to sound actionable enough to guide real choices, not just describe ideals.
